title: The Goophered Grapevine
focus: a story told to protect a livelihood

teacherSummary.text: A white Northerner, John, considers buying a run-down North Carolina vineyard. Julius McAdoo, a formerly enslaved man, tells him it is 'goophered' (conjured): before the war, an enslaved man named Henry ate its grapes, and his life rose and fell with the vines until he died. John buys anyway and later suspects Julius told the tale because he profited from the grapes; he hires Julius as coachman.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “The Goophered Grapevine,” how does Chesnutt show a story told to protect a livelihood? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In The Goophered Grapevine, how does Chesnutt develop the idea of a story told to protect a livelihood? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the point of view in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how The Goophered Grapevine develops the idea of a story told to protect a livelihood. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of The Goophered Grapevine (where it begins, turns and ends) and its point of view shape the reader's understanding of a story told to protect a livelihood. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what The Goophered Grapevine suggests about a story told to protect a livelihood. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's point of view and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay. Distinguish what is directly stated from what is really meant.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Charles W. Chesnutt uses point of view in The Goophered Grapevine to complicate the reader's understanding of a story told to protect a livelihood. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate The Goophered Grapevine within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of a story told to protect a livelihood responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read The Goophered Grapevine alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of a story told to protect a livelihood follows or bends those conventions, using the point of view as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to The Goophered Grapevine and its treatment of a story told to protect a livelihood. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's point of view and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads The Goophered Grapevine as evidence for a larger claim about a story told to protect a livelihood in The Goophered Grapevine. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads The Goophered Grapevine as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of a story told to protect a livelihood. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on The Goophered Grapevine.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why might someone tell a story that is not literally true? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes slavery; heavy dialect; a racial slur used by the characters.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are desuetude, trellises, shiftless, monologue, shyness. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Several planters thereabouts had attempted it on a commercial scale, in former years, with greater or less success; but like most Southern industries, it had felt the blight of war and had fallen into desuetude.” In this sentence it means: a state of disuse; no longer being used or kept up. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of The Goophered Grapevine would have known. Published in The Atlantic Monthly in 1887, the first story by an African American writer in that magazine; collected in The Conjure Woman (1899). Why does this story matter? Chesnutt reworks the 'plantation tradition' frame to expose slavery's cruelty and Black economic agency. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “We found the weather delightful at that season, the end of summer, and were hospitably entertained.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to a story told to protect a livelihood? I circle “hospitably”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find point of view, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for point of view.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: We found the weather delightful at that season, the end of summer, and were hospitably entertained. Our host was a man of means and evidently regarded our visit as a pleasure, and we were therefore correspondingly at our ease, and in a position to act with the coolness of judgment desirable in making so radical a change in our lives. My cousin placed a horse and buggy at our disposal, and himself acted as our guide until I became somewhat familiar with the country.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Point of view, Diction / vocabulary, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how The Goophered Grapevine develops the idea of a story told to protect a livelihood. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and diction / vocabulary shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to slavery and its memory? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about a story told to protect a livelihood, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how point of view shapes a story told to protect a livelihood. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
